summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for generic forward error correction of media data, based on XOR parity. It supports different protection lengths, levels and group sizes to suit various media and networks. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Every few packets, send an extra packet that is a mix of the others. If one gets lost, the receiver can work it out from the mix.

questions: how does xor parity fec work
how does uneven level protection work
subtitle: Send extra XOR packets alongside real-time RTP media so receivers can rebuild lost packets without asking for a resend.

tldr.problem: Real-time audio and video cannot wait for retransmissions, so lost RTP packets need to be repaired from information the sender already included.
tldr.mechanism: The sender XORs groups of media packets into FEC packets. Each FEC packet says which media packets it covers and how many bytes at each protection level, so the start of a packet can get stronger protection than the rest.
tldr.outcome: This replaces RFC 2733 and RFC 3009 and is not backward compatible with them. Media packets are untouched, so receivers without FEC support can simply ignore the extra packets.

facts.label: Longest group
facts.value: 16 packets, or 48 with the long mask

facts.label: Minimum rate
facts.value: Above 1000 Hz as a separate stream

today: RFC 5109 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 2733 and RFC 3009, and its FEC is not backward compatible with them, so the RFC recommends that existing implementations of those be updated to this specification when possible.

sections.title: Why Real-Time Media Needs FEC
sections.content:
Real-time applications have strict delay requirements, so retransmitting lost packets is generally not a valid option. The RFC points to Forward Error Correction (FEC) instead: the sender adds redundant data up front so the receiver can recover from loss on its own.

This document extends the FEC of RFC 2733 and RFC 3009 with unequal error protection and fixes an inconsistency in them: those RFCs used the P, X and CC fields of the RTP header in ways that differ from how RTP defines them, which prevented a payload-independent validity check of RTP packets.

The format is called generic because it is independent of the media type, flexible across FEC configurations, adaptable without out-of-band signaling, and usable with several ways of transporting the FEC packets.
sections.eli5: If you are talking live, you cannot ask a friend to repeat every word you missed. So the sender mails a little extra hint with the words, and you use the hint to fill in the gaps.

sections.title: XOR Parity and Uneven Level Protection
sections.content:
The scheme is built on the exclusive-or (XOR) operation. The RFC's example: for media packets a, b, c, d, the sender also sends f(a,b) and f(c,d). That is a 50% overhead, but if b is lost, a and f(a,b) recover it. A bigger group size means less overhead but weaker protection. The RFC chose XOR over codes such as Reed-Solomon because of its simplicity, which matters for nodes with limited resources.

Many media streams put the most important data at the beginning of each packet. Uneven Level Protection (ULP) splits packets into sections of decreasing importance called levels. Each level is protected independently, and lower levels can use smaller groups of packets for stronger protection. A single FEC packet can carry parity data for several levels, and the length protected at each level is the protection length, which can change during a session.

In the RFC's example, FEC packet #1 protects packets A and B at level 0 only. FEC packet #2 protects C and D at level 0 and all of A to D at level 1.
sections.eli5: Imagine a letter where the first lines matter most. You make two backup copies of the first lines and only one backup of the rest. If part of the letter is smudged, you are most likely to get the important beginning back.

sections.title: The FEC Packet Format
sections.content:
Media packets are not changed by FEC, which is why receivers without FEC support still work. An FEC packet is an RTP header, then a 10-octet FEC header, then one or more levels, each with a level header and a level payload.

The FEC header holds the E bit (extension flag, set to 0 and ignored by receivers), the L bit (short 16-bit mask when 0, long 48-bit mask when 1), recovery fields for the P, X, CC, M and PT values, an SN base (the lowest protected sequence number), a 32-bit TS recovery field and a 16-bit length recovery field. The length recovery field lets packets of different sizes be recovered.

Each level header is a 16-bit protection length plus the mask. If bit i of the mask is 1, the media packet with sequence number N + i is protected, where N is the SN base. So a group can span at most 16 packets, or 48 with the long mask.

Three rules keep levels simple: a packet is protected only once at each level above 0 (level 0 may protect it more than once if the level 0 protection lengths are equal), a packet protected at level p must also be protected at level p-1, and an FEC packet with level p must also contain level p-1.

When FEC travels in a separate stream, the RTP header follows RFC 3550 with some clarifications: the marker is 0, the SSRC equals the protected stream's SSRC, the sequence number goes up by one per FEC packet, and the timestamp is the media clock at transmission time.
sections.eli5: Each backup packet carries a note saying which packets it covers and how many bytes of each it protects. The receiver reads the note to know which packets to combine.

sections.title: Building and Using the Parity
sections.content:
The FEC header values come from the bitwise XOR of an 80-bit protected bit string taken from each level 0 media packet: the first 64 bits of its RTP header plus a 16-bit length (the packet length in bytes minus 12 for the fixed RTP header). The FEC payload at each level is the XOR of the protected media packets, with shorter packets padded at the end with zero octets. At level n, only Ln octets are used, starting at octet Sn + 13, where Sn is the sum of the lower level lengths. The first 12 octets are skipped because the FEC header already covers them. Other procedures are allowed if the end result is identical.

Recovery has two steps. Working out which packets to combine can use any algorithm the implementer chooses. The reconstruction itself must follow the RFC: XOR the available media packets with the FEC data, then rebuild the RTP header (version 2, the lost packet's sequence number, the SSRC of the protected stream) and the payload level by level.

Because of unequal protection, a lost packet may be recovered in full or only in part. Partial recovery is detected by comparing the recovered length from the FEC header with the length of the data actually recovered.
sections.eli5: The backup packet is made by mixing packets together in a fixed way. To fix a missing one, you take the backup, mix in the packets you still have, and what is left over is the missing piece.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through bit-level examples with four media packets A to D, using sequence numbers 8 to 11 and payload lengths of 200, 140, 100 and 340 bytes.

In the single-level example, one FEC packet protects all four packets. The mask is 61440, the level 0 protection length is 340 (the longest packet), and the length recovery value is 372, which is 200 XOR 140 XOR 100 XOR 340.

In the two-level example, L0 is 70 and L1 is 90. FEC packet #1 covers A and B at level 0 (mask 49152). FEC packet #2 covers C and D at level 0 (mask 12288) and all four packets at level 1 (mask 61440).

A third example sends FEC as redundant coding with five media packets. FEC data protecting A to D rides in the fifth packet alongside media packet E. The FEC data is built from virtual RTP packets, made by removing the redundancy headers and replacing the payload type with that of the primary coding.
sections.eli5: The examples are like showing your work in math class: real packet sizes, real numbers, and the exact bits for each backup packet.

sections.title: Sending FEC and Signaling It
sections.content:
FEC packets can be sent in two main ways, and the choice is signaled out of band, for example with SDP. Dynamic payload types must be used because there is no static assignment for FEC.

Separate stream: the FEC stream uses the same SSRC as the protected stream. The RFC says the two SHOULD go in separate RTP sessions and MUST NOT be multiplexed by SSRC into one session, since they always share the same SSRC. SDP media line grouping with FEC semantics (RFC 3388 and RFC 4756) associates the streams, and the codec name is ulpfec.

Redundant encoding: FEC rides as a secondary codec in RFC 2198 redundant packets, and it MUST protect only the main codec. The marker bit is lost in that format, with or without FEC.

The media subtypes audio/ulpfec, video/ulpfec, text/ulpfec and application/ulpfec are registered with IANA. They need a rate parameter (above 1000 Hz when used as a separate stream) and take an optional onelevelonly parameter, whose default is 0. In offer/answer, an answerer may refuse FEC while still accepting the media.
sections.eli5: You can mail the backup notes in a separate envelope, or tuck them into the same envelope as the next message. Either way, you tell your friend ahead of time which method you are using.

sections.title: Security and Congestion
sections.content:
FEC can be applied to already encrypted payloads, mainly with SRTP, or before encryption. Because FEC is just XOR across the payload, FEC packets are as cryptographically secure as the original payload. When encryption is used, applications SHOULD encrypt both the media and FEC streams, and different keys MUST be used for each stream when they are sent separately. Key changes need care, because an FEC packet may protect packets encrypted under old and new keys.

Tampering with FEC data can badly affect recovery: changing the length recovery field can produce a recovered packet that is too long, and recovery effort can rise by at least one order of magnitude. The RFC suggests sanity checks before and after recovery.

On congestion, adding FEC when losses rise can make congestion worse. Implementations MUST NOT substantially increase the total bandwidth in use, payload plus FEC, as network losses increase. Best-effort users MUST monitor packet loss, and loss is acceptable only if a TCP flow on the same path would get at least the same average throughput.
sections.eli5: Locking up the backup notes matters as much as locking up the message, since someone could change a note to confuse you. Also, sending lots of backups when the road is jammed only makes the jam worse.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: Extension flag; set to 0 and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: 0 for a 16-bit mask, 1 for a 48-bit mask.

fields.name: P rec.
fields.desc: Recovery bit for the RTP padding bit.

fields.name: X rec.
fields.desc: Recovery bit for the RTP extension bit.

fields.name: CC rec.
fields.desc: Recovery field for the CSRC count.

fields.name: PT rec.
fields.desc: Recovery field for the payload type.

fields.name: SN base
fields.desc: Lowest sequence number protected at any level.

fields.name: TS recovery
fields.desc: XOR of the timestamps of the protected packets.

fields.name: Length recovery
fields.desc: XOR of the protected packets' lengths.

fields.name: Protection Length
fields.desc: Bytes of data protected at this level.

fields.name: Mask
fields.desc: Bit i set means media packet N + i is protected, N being the SN base.
